\title{What do source models buy? Design-based benchmark prediction from a few items}
\author{Anonymous Author(s)}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Methods that predict a model's full-benchmark score from a few items, using the item-level results of earlier \emph{source} models, are usually validated on models that resemble the sources.
We treat the task as estimating a finite-population mean with the source matrix as a covariate: the sources can reduce the variance through the choice of items and the estimator, while the bias must be controlled by the design.
On 13 binary item-by-model matrices, three splits of models into sources and targets (random models, held-out families, targets above every source) and seven designs combined with model-based, plug-in and difference estimators, we ask what the sources buy at $n=100$ items.
When targets resemble the sources, the method classes chosen without looking at the outcomes reach $0.65$--$0.79$ of the RMSE of uniform sampling and $0.80$--$0.94$ of that of stratified sampling.
For targets above every source, IRT and kNN predictors are worse than uniform sampling ($1.96$ and $2.42$ times its RMSE) because they compress their estimates toward the source mean; a difference correction reduces this bias without removing it, and the only class clearly below stratified sampling, by about a tenth of its error, pairs a balanced design with calibrated regression.
The gain needs many source models and does not carry over to the ordering of models above the sources.
Anchor-point selection, in our re-implementation, is not clearly better than uniform sampling.
\end{abstract}


\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Running a language model on every item of a large benchmark is costly, and the cost recurs with every new model.
A growing line of work therefore evaluates a model on a small subset of $n\ll N$ items and predicts its full-benchmark score, using the item-level results that earlier \emph{source} models already provide~\citep{vivek2024anchor,maiapolo2024tiny,kipnis2025metabench,pacchiardi2024100,li2025active}.
These methods choose the items from the source matrix, by clustering or by item-response-theory (IRT) information, and read the target's score off a latent model fitted on the sources.
They are validated mostly on held-out models that resemble the sources, entangle the choice of items with the choice of estimator, and are rarely compared with simple sampling that uses the sources only to spread the items over difficulty.

We ask what the source models buy.
Our frame is finite-population estimation: the target's full score is the mean of $N$ unknown binary values, the source matrix is a covariate known for every item, and a sample of $n$ items is drawn by a design.
In that frame the sources can reduce the \emph{variance} of the estimate, through the design and through the estimator, while the \emph{bias} must be controlled by the design: items are drawn with probabilities bounded away from zero, and a correction by the target's own residuals makes the estimator unbiased when its predictor is fixed in advance.
It separates whether a predictor fitted on the sources is accurate where the target resembles them from whether it stays accurate when the target is stronger than every source, as a new frontier model is.

shown.message:
I read the revised Outline and Brief, and my local text already agrees with their account of the recalibrated estimator and the weak-prior check. They also state a main finding that the abstract and introduction lacked, so I added it. In extrapolation, the design and the estimator draw on the same source information, and they do not add. A target-recalibrated regression on a stratified or balanced design is within 3% of the plain mean on that design.

The commits are local on `dev` and unpushed. They cite Table 10 and Appendix `app:recal`, and the table is still with `figtab-repo` (#8). I haven't built the PDF or checked the nine-page limit with the new sentences.

When Table 10 arrives I will check the build and the page limit, then push and open the `dev` into `main` PR. Version `final` also waits on the public-baseline comparison (M6) from `experiment-repo`.
